newsitem.title: UK: Britain says German jobless rise shows EU dangers.
newsitem.headline: Britain says German jobless rise shows EU dangers.

text.p: Britain's Trade secretary Ian Lang said on Thursday that a surge in German unemployment figures showed European social policies were not working.

Attacking the opposition Labour party, which he said would copy German policies and put British jobs at risk, Lang said: "Last month half a million Germans lost their jobs. That dramatic rise in German unemployment is a stark warning to Britain of the dangers threatened by New Labour's plans to copy German employment policies.
"It is also a total vindication of the Prime Minister's warning to Europe on Tuesday that continental social policies are destroying jobs, while in Conservative Britain we are creating them."
Lang's statement followed Thursday's announcement that German unemployment surged by over a half a million to a post-war record of 4.66 million in January.
The aim of the statement, issued by ruling Conservative party headquarters, was to bolster Prime Minister John Major's efforts to cut Labour's opinion poll lead of around 20 points.
With less than three months before an election, time is running out for Major to stage a comeback and extend his Conservative party's unbroken 18 year rule.

Major, who has lost his overall majority in parliament through deaths and defections, has been forced to harden his line on Europe due to pressure from so-called Eurosceptics in his party bitterly opposed to any moves to European integration.

Labour has matched most of Major's policies on Europe, promising a referendum before taking Britain into a European single currency and saying that British entry into the single currency when it starts in 1999 is unlikely.

But Major appears to have decided to make Europe his battleground, convinced his opposition to the social chapter -- which sets workplace standards across the bloc -- and Labour's pledge to sign up is a key difference which could sway voters.
Two days ago, Major used a speech in Brussels to warn that British dole queues could lengthen by 500,000 if Labour took power and signed up to the social chapter.
Labour immediately hit back. The opposition's foreign affairs spokesman, Robin Cook, said: "There is nothing in the social chapter which threatens British competitiveness..."
But whatever the effect at home, Lang's comments are unlikely to be welcomed in Germany, which has been growing increasingly impatient with Major's strident anti-European line.
